Lee-Carter model

Source: R/model-lee_carter.R
lee_carter.Rd

log m[x, t] = a[x] + b[x] k[t] with the constraints sum(b) = 1 and sum(k) = 0, fitted per stratum:

Usage

lee_carter(
  method = c("poisson", "svd"),
  jump_off = c("fitted", "observed"),
  bootstrap = FALSE,
  n_boot = 100,
  adjust = c("dt", "dxt", "e0", "none"),
  choose_period = FALSE,
  min_years = 20,
  rotate = FALSE,
  rotation = c(e0_start = 80, e0_end = 102, power = 0.5)
)

Arguments

method

"poisson" or "svd".

jump_off

"fitted" (forecasts start from the fitted rates of the last year) or "observed" (from the observed rates of the last year).

bootstrap

Semi-parametric bootstrap of the parameters.

n_boot

Number of bootstrap fits.

adjust

Re-estimation of k[t] for method = "svd": "dt", "dxt", "e0" or "none".

choose_period

Choose the fitting period (Booth, Maindonald and Smith 2002).

min_years

choose_period considers fitting periods of more than min_years years (minperiod of demography::lca()).

rotate

Rotate the age pattern of decline b towards an ultimate pattern as life expectancy at birth rises (Li, Lee and Gerland 2013).

rotation

Settings of the rotation, a named vector: life expectancy at birth at which the rotation starts (e0_start) and is complete (e0_end), and the exponent of the weights (power). The defaults are those of Li, Lee and Gerland (2013) and MortCast; elements left out keep their defaults.

Value

A model specification.

Details

  • method = "poisson": Poisson log-bilinear model (Brouhns, Denuit and Vermunt 2002), maximum likelihood by Newton updates;

  • method = "svd": original method (Lee and Carter 1992): singular value decomposition of centred log rates, with k[t] re-estimated in a second stage (adjust, as in demography::lca()): so that the fitted deaths match the observed total deaths of each year ("dt", Lee and Carter 1992), by Poisson maximum likelihood of the deaths by age given a and b ("dxt", Booth, Maindonald and Smith 2002), so that the fitted life expectancy at the first age matches the observed one ("e0", Lee and Miller 2001), or not at all ("none").

choose_period = TRUE fits the model to the last years only, starting in the year that minimises the ratio of the mean deviance of a fit with a linear k[t] to the mean deviance of the Lee-Carter fit (Booth, Maindonald and Smith 2002): the longest recent period over which the decline was close to linear (demography::lca(chooseperiod = TRUE, breakmethod = "bms") gives the same period). Fitted rates of earlier years are missing.

Compared with demography::lca(), k[t] is centred again after the second stage (a constant shift of k and a, with identical fitted rates), and life tables use a_x = n/2 at age 0 (as life_table()), so adjust = "e0" matches a slightly different life expectancy than demography's life table where age 0 is in the data.

The period index follows a random walk with drift. Draws include the innovations and the uncertainty of the drift. With bootstrap = TRUE the parameters are re-estimated on n_boot Poisson resamples of the fitted deaths of the fitting period (semi-parametric bootstrap of Brouhns et al. 2005), which adds the uncertainty of a and b.

Age groups without deaths in the fitting period get a constant rate (0.5 deaths over the period) and no trend; with adjust = "e0" they enter the life tables at that rate.

rotate = TRUE rotates the age pattern of decline as life expectancy rises (Li, Lee and Gerland 2013). In long-lived populations the decline of mortality slows down at young ages and speeds up at old ages, which a fixed b[x] does not capture over long horizons. For each path and year t, the life expectancy at birth e0 of the unrotated forecast gives the weight w = (0.5 (1 + sin(pi / 2 (2 u - 1))))^power with u = (e0 - e0_start) / (e0_end - e0_start); w is 0 below e0_start and 1 from e0_end. The age pattern of that year is B[x, t] = (1 - w) b[x] + w bu[x]. The ultimate pattern bu has the mean of b over ages 15-64 at all ages below 65; from age 65 it keeps the shape of b, scaled so that the first age group from 65 equals that mean; it sums to 1 like b. The index is then solved again, path by path and year by year, so that the rotated rates have the same life expectancy at birth as the unrotated ones: rotation changes the age pattern of the forecast and keeps its life expectancy at birth. Decline thus moves from young ages to the ages where bu exceeds b. Where b at 65 is already above its mean over ages 15-64 (as for French women), it moves mostly to ages 15-64. Rates change from the jump-off year T, log m[x, t] = log m[x, T] + B[x, t] (k*[t] - k[T]), so the jump-off rates stay as they are. Fitted rates, and paths with e0 below e0_start, are unchanged. In MortCast (Sevcikova et al. 2016) the path of life expectancy comes from a separate model (bayesLife); here it is that of the Lee-Carter draws. Rotation needs ages from 0 (life expectancy at birth) with age groups starting at 15 and 65. With a closed last age group, a warning notes that life expectancy is then truncated at the highest age. Rotated forecasts compute life tables for every path and year and are much slower (about 20 times for single years of age).

References

Lee RD, Carter LR (1992). Modeling and forecasting U.S. mortality. Journal of the American Statistical Association 87(419): 659-671.

Brouhns N, Denuit M, Vermunt JK (2002). A Poisson log-bilinear regression approach to the construction of projected lifetables. Insurance: Mathematics and Economics 31(3): 373-393. doi:10.1016/S0167-6687(02)00185-3

Booth H, Maindonald J, Smith L (2002). Applying Lee-Carter under conditions of variable mortality decline. Population Studies 56(3): 325-336. doi:10.1080/00324720215935

Lee R, Miller T (2001). Evaluating the performance of the Lee-Carter method for forecasting mortality. Demography 38(4): 537-549. doi:10.1353/dem.2001.0036

Brouhns N, Denuit M, Van Keilegom I (2005). Bootstrapping the Poisson log-bilinear model for mortality forecasting. Scandinavian Actuarial Journal 2005(3): 212-224.

Li N, Lee R, Gerland P (2013). Extending the Lee-Carter method to model the rotation of age patterns of mortality decline for long-term projections. Demography 50(6): 2037-2051. doi:10.1007/s13524-013-0232-2

Sevcikova H, Li N, Kantorova V, Gerland P, Raftery AE (2016). Age-specific mortality and fertility rates for probabilistic population projections. In Schoen R (ed.) Dynamic Demographic Analysis. Springer, 285-310. doi:10.1007/978-3-319-26603-9_15

Examples

x <- mt_example(deaths = "single")
fit <- mt_fit(lee_carter(), x)
fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 10, n_draws = 200, seed = 1)
# \donttest{
# rotation needs ages from 0: French women (HMD, via demography)
if (requireNamespace("demography", quietly = TRUE)) {
  fr <- as_mt_data(demography::fr.mort, series = "female", years = 1970:2006)
  fr <- mt_regroup(fr, age = c(0, 1, seq(5, 100, 5)))
  fc_rot <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(lee_carter(rotate = TRUE), fr), h = 50, n_draws = 100, seed = 1)
  life_expectancy(fc_rot)
}
